evals.prompt: I'm organising BuildJam, a 36-hour hackathon for about 120 people in Trondheim this November. Nordvik Systems is my employer and they signed off a Prizes line of 40,000 NOK in the event budget. No sponsors so far. I want to hand out 20,000 / 12,000 / 8,000 in cash to first, second and third. Does that split look right, or should I weight the top more heavily?
evals.expected_output: A response that stops the sizing conversation, settles the prize medium first, argues against cash as the default, presents the five-rung medium menu with its efficiency ordering, keeps the pool inside the 40,000 NOK Prizes line, and asks the minor / cross-border / legal-entity questions before recommending a split.
expectations: Addresses the prize medium (cash versus non-cash) before sizing or splitting the pool, and says explicitly that the medium decision comes first
Presents a five-rung medium menu containing cash, gear, credits or vouchers, opportunity, and recognition only
Names gear - hardware, components, tools the winner keeps - as the recommended default rather than cash
Cites MLH's stated position that it does not recommend cash prizes and that the perceived value of a cash prize is lower than traditional prizes
Flags that the anti-cash claim is one organisation's stated position rather than a measured comparison of outcomes
States an efficiency ordering of the medium menu that places cash fourth, below gear, recognition only and credits
Explains that cash is cheapest to procure but most expensive on the compliance axis, rather than calling cash the cheapest option outright
Treats the 40,000 NOK Prizes line as a ceiling the pool must fit inside, and proposes no pool above it
Names graduated podium as the default split shape rather than weighting the top more heavily
States no tax-form name, no numeric tax or reporting threshold, and no jurisdictional currency trigger anywhere in the response
Asks whether any winner could be a minor or located outside the organiser's country, and whether the organising team has its own legal entity or a fiscal host
Does not present cash as the obviously correct answer merely because the user proposed it

evals.prompt: Kestrel Labs here. Our hackathon finished Saturday and the judges have ranked everyone. The winning team has a 16-year-old on it. Second place is three people who flew in from Buenos Aires - we're registered in Dublin. Prizes are 2,000 EUR for first and 1,000 EUR for second, and I was going to just do bank transfers this week. What do I need from each of them before I send the money?
evals.expected_output: A response that names the live exposure categories without answering any of them, treats the minor and the cross-border winner as gates forcing review before announcement or payment, deletes cash and informal handover for this event, gives the cheapest-first routing ladder, and states no threshold, form name or percentage.
expectations: Names the minor-receiving-an-award exposure category and routes it rather than answering it
Names the cross-border payment exposure category and routes it rather than answering it
Names payer-side tax reporting and withholding as a category, and states it typically attaches to the organiser rather than to the winner
States that the specific threshold, form or requirement is jurisdiction-specific
States no numeric tax threshold, no tax-form name, and no withholding percentage anywhere in the response
Treats the minor and the cross-border winner as gates forcing a counsel or fiscal-host review before the prize is announced or paid, not as factors weighed against effort
Deletes cash from the medium menu for this event rather than demoting it, on the grounds that a minor and a winner outside the organiser's country are both in the pool
Deletes informal handover from the payout-rigor menu because the prize is cash
Separates cross-border payment into two distinct problems: whether the payment rail can reach the winner at all, and what rules or treaty questions apply to the outbound payment
Notes that the organiser's bank or platform answers the reachability question but not the rules question
Gives a routing ladder ordered cheapest-first: published practice, then the fiscal host or institution holding the money, then the funding sponsor's legal team, then counsel
Does not re-open or alter the judges' ranking
Distinguishes the minor payout question from an overnight-stay or venue waiver for a minor

evals.prompt: Quick one. Two of our mentors hacked on a side project overnight and the judges put them second. Separately, one of the engineers from Aeroleaf, who paid 8,000 for our Aeroleaf API Challenge track, was on the team that won that exact track. Our published rules only say the event is open to everyone. What's the right call on both?
evals.expected_output: A response that splits eligibility to compete from eligibility to receive, applies published practice to the mentors, treats the sponsor-employee case as a routed exposure category distinct from judging conflict of interest, supplies wording that grants building and withholds winning separately, and leaves the ranking untouched.
expectations: Distinguishes eligibility to compete from eligibility to receive as two different permissions
States that mentors may be permitted to build and demo a project while still being ineligible to receive a prize
Cites published practice excluding volunteers, organizers and mentors from winning prizes while allowing them to work on projects for their portfolio
Names the sponsor-employee-receiving-their-own-sponsor's-track-prize exposure category
States that the sponsor-employee payout question is distinct from the judging conflict of interest that governs who decides the rank
Routes the sponsor-employee question to the signed sponsorship agreement first, then to the sponsor's own legal team or counsel
Notes the sponsor-employee question should have been settled in the sponsorship agreement before the event
Does not re-open or change the judges' placements
Rejects wording of the form 'organizers and volunteers may not participate' as ambiguous between may-not-build and may-not-win
Provides eligibility-to-receive wording that grants permission to build and withholds permission to win in separate clauses
Hands the eligibility text to the hackathon brief or published rules document rather than publishing it from here
Notes that the published 'open to everyone' rule left the receiving question unanswered, and that the organiser decides it rather than a template supplying it

evals.prompt: We're giving each placing team a set of components - a dev kit, a soldering station and a multimeter per person. Team size cap in the rules is 4, so I ordered 4 of each for first and 4 for second. First place turned out to be 3 people, and one of them brought a friend on Sunday morning who isn't on the submission. I still have to decide second and third - can I just do a 50/30/20 style split like we did with cash last year?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to apply a cash percentage split to gear, plans in whole units against the team-size cap, sets a leftover-unit rule in advance, resolves the unlisted fifth person by publishing whether the award follows the roster or the people present, and flags backorder risk.
expectations: States that a non-cash prize is counted in units per person while cash divides arbitrarily, so a percentage split does not transfer to gear
Plans the split in whole units against the published team-size cap rather than as percentages
Requires a stated rule for the leftover unit decided before the event rather than improvised at the podium
Names concrete leftover options such as returned, raffled, or held for a later edition
Cites the practice of saving prize receipts so an unused unit can be returned and added to a later budget
Requires publishing whether the award follows the submitted team roster or the people present, which resolves the late-joining friend
Does not award a unit to the unlisted fifth person on the strength of their attendance alone
Warns that gear should be ordered early because many items are backordered, framing it as vendor-side stock risk rather than a shipping deadline
Recommends recording what was actually handed over, to whom, and what remains outstanding
Does not apply a cash percentage split to the component prizes

evals.prompt: Two things. Halcyon Grid told me on a call they'll fund a 10,000 USD prize for their track - nothing signed yet - and I want to put it on the site Monday because registration opens then. Second, Merribell is donating 5 seats of their platform, they say list price is 2,400 USD each, so I want to make that 12,000 USD bundle the grand prize and push Merribell's own track to third. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A response that blocks publication of the unsigned sponsor prize, refuses the retail valuation of the donated seats, classifies the seats as credits with the compliance consequences and redemption failure points that follow, warns about in-kind podium ordering, and asks when the sponsor money actually clears.
expectations: Refuses to publish or announce the Halcyon Grid prize before the sponsorship is signed, and names an unsigned-but-announced prize as a failure mode the organiser ends up owning personally
States that the organiser's own baseline pool and the sponsor-funded part are separate, with different ceilings and different owners
Rejects valuing the Merribell donation at its stated list price
Notes that valuing in-kind at the budget line it displaces assumes the organiser would otherwise have made that spend, and that the assumption must be checked before applying it to a prize
Warns that podium order does not track perceived value for in-kind prizes, so a third-place item can be worth more to its winner than a first-place one
Treats the platform seats as credits or vouchers rather than as gear
Places credits beside cash rather than beside gear on the compliance axis, because redeemable value is treated like a cash equivalent for reporting purposes
Requires publishing the credit's expiry date, redemption region, and any account the winner must create
Asks when the sponsor money actually clears, and flags that a sponsorship clearing after the event means the organiser funds the prize personally in the meantime
States no currency amount as a recommended reporting threshold or tax trigger anywhere in the response
Names the sponsor-funded pool as the default rung where a sponsor is in play, while conditioning it on signed commitments rather than verbal ones
Does not treat the verbal commitment as equivalent to a signed one

evals.prompt: Bramblewick Hack, third edition. We've got three sponsor tracks signed - each sponsor put up 5k for their own track - plus a general best overall category already published in the brief. Last year we did one grand prize and nothing else and it kept the ceremony short. I want to do that again: one winner, one big award. Two organisers, both part-time, so simplicity matters a lot to us.
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes winner-take-most because signed sponsor tracks leave it nowhere to put a sponsor award, recommends graduated podium with an award count covering each track, cites the many-chances-to-win guidance, and uses the low effort ceiling to keep the flat split starved.
expectations: Deletes winner-take-most from the split menu because sponsors fund named tracks and the shape has nowhere to put a sponsor award
Deletes rather than merely demotes winner-take-most, and attributes the deletion to the signed sponsor tracks
Names graduated podium as the default split shape
Cites published organizer guidance that splitting a pool into many chances to win is the most effective structure because participants want a reasonable chance of placing before committing hours
States that winner-take-most motivates only the teams who already believe they can win
Ranks track-only below graduated podium on value, because with no overall award a team that used no sponsor's product has nothing to aim at
Notes that the already-published best overall category means track-only would contradict the published brief
Names flat-across-many-tracks as the starved option, top of every cost axis
States the flat option's promotion condition as several published sponsor tracks plus a non-cash medium
Uses the two part-time organisers' low effort ceiling as a reason not to promote the flat split, whose cost is the per-winner check repeated
Gives an explicit award count for the recommended shape
Does not collapse the three sponsor tracks into a single combined award

evals.prompt: Torvik Open. Last edition we got 40 project submissions and I want way more this time. My thinking is a 50,000 USD headline pool - that's the kind of number that gets written about. Our finance person hasn't put a Prizes figure in the budget yet, she says tell her what you need. How should I size and pitch it?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes the flagship pool because the Prizes line does not exist, presents the bigger-pool-draws-more-submissions claim as an untested assumption, cites the counter-guidance and the single-edition illustrations with their limits, and refuses to name a figure for finance to adopt.
expectations: Deletes the flagship pool option because the budget's Prizes line has not been set
States that a headline pool sized against no ceiling commits money on behalf of a budget nobody has written
Presents 'a bigger pool draws more submissions' as an untested assumption rather than an established fact
Cites published organizer guidance that a modest, well-distributed pool can perform as well as a much larger one
Cites published guidance that more prize money is no guarantee of stronger submissions
Notes the counterpart finding that a very low prize can suppress participation
Cites the ETHGlobal Bangkok figures - roughly 713 project submissions from about 1,950 hackers in its largest-ever prize pool edition - as a single-edition illustration rather than as evidence
States that the cited large-pool editions do not control for year-over-year growth and publish no same-edition comparison against a smaller pool
Notes that leading with a headline pool competes on ground credible large events deliberately vacate by leading with learning, building and sharing
Warns that a headline pool selects for the participants who came for the money
Asks whether the prize is meant to buy attention before the event or reward winners after it, and ties the flagship promotion condition to that intent
Requires the Prizes line to exist before any pool is proposed, rather than naming a figure for finance to adopt

evals.prompt: Four of us run a free weekend hack night in Ghent - no company, no nonprofit, we just pass a hat for pizza. Someone offered us 500 EUR and we want to hand it to whoever builds the best thing. One of us would take the cash and pay it out from their personal account. Anything we should watch for?
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes cash because there is no legal entity and no fiscal host, refuses the personal-account route, promotes recognition only as a deliberate structure, names the fiscal-sponsorship route with its operational questions, and states no threshold or form name.
expectations: Deletes cash from the medium menu because the organising team has no legal entity and no fiscal host
Declines the personal-account payout route rather than treating it as an acceptable workaround
Promotes recognition only, naming it as the one rung that needs neither a legal entity nor a fiscal host
Frames recognition only as a deliberately chosen structure rather than a fallback or a downgrade
Suggests a recognition form that outlives the ceremony, such as a trophy passed between cohorts or a public acknowledgement from someone the winners recognise
Names fiscal sponsorship as the standard route for an organising team with no entity of its own
Names Hack Club and Hack+ as hackathon-specific fiscal sponsors

Lists the operational questions to ask any host: who holds signing authority and how long their review takes, where funds are held and what fees apply, and the timeline between money arriving and being spendable
States no numeric threshold, tax-form name, or reporting figure
Cites a civic-tech organizer's published practice of running hackathons without making winners and losers
Offers a non-cash medium that avoids the payment rail entirely as an alternative to routing the 500 EUR

evals.prompt: Lumenpath Hack. Plan is cash envelopes handed over on stage at the closing ceremony - fast, no paperwork, everyone goes home happy. We also want to make prizes conditional on the winners keeping their repo public so the community benefits. Write that up for me.
evals.expected_output: A response that deletes informal handover because the prize is cash, sets standard-form payout as the default with its claim step described as a category rather than a document, explains why deferring the review to handover is the expensive option, and bounds the continuing condition with a finality date and a failure rule.
expectations: Deletes informal handover from the payout-rigor menu because the prize is cash
Names standard-form payout as the default payout rung
Describes standard-form payout as published eligibility-to-receive text, a claim step, and identity or status collection appropriate to the medium
Explains that informal handover is not the cheapest option on compliance because it defers the whole review to the least reversible moment, after money has reached a stranger
States that a misjudged rank can be re-announced while a payment cannot be un-made
Requires publishing the date the award becomes final alongside any continuing condition
Requires publishing what happens to the prize if the condition fails after the handover
Warns that a continuing condition with no stated end leaves every award permanently revocable
Cites published rules making prize eligibility conditional on the submission staying public, with new winners selectable if it is not
Notes the continuing condition costs far more on a cash prize than on a trophy or other recognition award
Describes what the winner must provide as a category rather than naming a specific document or form

evals.prompt: Judging wrapped an hour ago. Quarrystone came first, but Vantwell is the team our biggest sponsor has been raving about all weekend - could we rework the split so Vantwell's second-place award lands close to first? Also, our booth raffle winner should get something out of the prize pool, and we planned to reveal the whole prize structure during the closing ceremony as a surprise. Fine?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to reshape the split toward a sponsor favourite, keeps the raffle out of the competition prize pool and routes it to sponsor fulfillment, and rejects revealing the structure at the ceremony because publication must precede submissions closing.
expectations: Refuses to reshape the split to move value toward Vantwell, and names it as re-judging by another route
States that the ranked outcome is an input to be awarded against, and that prize size must never influence who won
Separates the booth raffle from the competition prize, stating a raffle is an attendee incentive open to any attendee while a competition prize is awarded on a judged rank
Routes the booth raffle to sponsor fulfillment rather than funding it from the competition prize pool
Rejects revealing the prize structure at the closing ceremony, and requires publication before submissions close
States that a prize announced after teams have chosen what to build has already failed at motivating anything
Notes the eligibility questions differ between a raffle and a judged award even though both are sponsor-funded and both get called a prize
Recommends recording what was actually handed over, to whom, and what remains outstanding
Does not propose a discretionary or special award invented after the fact to satisfy the sponsor's preference
Presents the structure for validation before anything reaches the published brief, treating publication as the point of no return

evals.prompt: Oakcrest Devfest hackathon. Registration opens Monday and I need the prize section written. Facts: the budget's Prizes line is 3,000 EUR. Two sponsor tracks signed and paid - Ferrowyn and Stilbeck, 1,500 EUR each. We've decided on hardware kits. Team cap is 4. One registrant is 17. We're a registered nonprofit with a treasurer who signs. Give me the finished text.
evals.expected_output: A prize structure presented section by section against a six-item completeness check, separating the organiser's line from the sponsor money, planning kits in whole units with a leftover rule, treating the 17-year-old as a gate, and shipping eligibility wording with no unresolved brackets.
expectations: Enumerates a six-item completeness check covering the medium, the total pool with its budget line, the split with an award count, the eligibility-to-receive text, the payout mechanic naming who hands over what, and the list of exposure categories with who each was routed to
States that all six must exist in writing with zero blanks before the brief is published, and iterates until the count is six
Separates the organiser's 3,000 EUR Prizes line from the 3,000 EUR of signed sponsor track funding rather than merging them into one pool
Treats the 17-year-old registrant as a gate requiring a counsel or fiscal-host review before the prize is announced, not as a menu weighting traded off against effort
States no numeric age threshold, tax-form name, or reporting figure, and says the minor question is jurisdiction-specific
Delivers eligibility-to-receive wording with every bracketed decision resolved, and states that publishing a paragraph with a bracket left in is worse than publishing nothing
Hands the eligibility text to the hackathon brief or rules document rather than publishing it directly from here
Plans the hardware kits in whole units against the team cap of 4, with a stated leftover-unit rule
Names a split shape with an explicit award count that accommodates both signed sponsor tracks
Presents the structure section by section - medium, pool, split, eligibility, payout mechanic - for validation before publication
Notes the nonprofit's signing authority and review time as an input to whether the payout can happen on schedule
